1 Introduction to inheritance

1.1 Shapes: “is a” and “has a”

You’re building software that draws 2D shapes: rectangles, squares, polygons, circles, ellipses… One class per shape? Wait a minute:

“Is a” relationships:

  • a Square is a Rectangle;
  • a Rectangle is a Polygon;
  • a Circle is an Ellipse;
  • all of them are Shapes.

“Has a” relationships:

  • a Polygon has a list of Point2Ds;
  • an Ellipse has a centre (a Point2D) and two axis lengths a and b;
  • a Circle is an Ellipse with a == b.

So why build all those classes separately? Drawing a square should just be drawing a rectangle with equal sides.

1.2 Hierarchies

A hierarchy is a diagram showing how things are related.

WarningWatch out

Everyday “is a” can mislead. A square is a rectangle, but if Rectangle has set_width(), a Square can’t honour it without breaking its own rules. This classic trap is the square–rectangle problem. In code, “is a” must mean “can be used anywhere the base class is used”.

1.3 The people of a university

If shapes don’t convince you, look at our university:

  • every staff member has a name, a birthday and an ID;
  • every student has a name, a birthday and an ID;
  • there are different kinds of staff: Lecturer, TOMember, Demonstrator, SecurityGuard;
  • and different kinds of students: UGStudent, PGTStudent (postgraduate taught), PGRStudent (postgraduate research).

Writing all seven classes separately means writing the common members seven times: copy, paste, repeat.

That breaks the golden rule from Chapter 02: Don’t Repeat Yourself.

1.4 A better design

What all people share goes in UniPerson; what all staff share goes in StaffMember; and each role adds only what’s special about it.

2 Basic inheritance in C++

2.1 Terminology

In an inheritance (“is a”) relationship:

  • the class being inherited from is the base class (or parent class, or superclass);
  • the class doing the inheriting is the derived class (or child class, or subclass).

2.2 A smaller example for our code

Every Lecturer and every Student is a UniPerson, with a name, an ID and an age. What they do differently comes with polymorphism, in Chapter 15.

2.3 The class UniPerson

uniperson.h
#ifndef UNIPERSON_H
#define UNIPERSON_H

#include <string>

class UniPerson {
  private:
    static inline int next_id{100000}; // ONE counter, shared by all
    std::string name{};
    int id{};
    int age{};

  public:
    UniPerson(const std::string& name = "", int age = 0)
        : name{name}, id{next_id++}, age{age} {}

    const std::string& get_name() const { return name; }
    int get_age() const { return age; }
    int get_id() const { return id; }
};

#endif

A static member variable belongs to the class, not to any one object: all UniPersons share one next_id. Each new person takes its value, then increments it.

inline (C++17) lets us initialize it right here, in the header.

2.4 Lecturer without inheritance

lecturer_noinheritance.cpp
#include <string>

class Lecturer { // no inheritance: everything written again
  private:
    static inline int next_id{100000}; // a SECOND, separate counter!
    std::string name{};
    int id{};
    int age{};
    double salary{};

  public:
    Lecturer(const std::string& name, int age, double salary)
        : name{name}, id{next_id++}, age{age}, salary{salary} {}

    const std::string& get_name() const { return name; } // copied...
    int get_age() const { return age; }                  // ...and
    int get_id() const { return id; }                    // pasted
    double get_salary() const { return salary; }
};

int main() {
    Lecturer khiem{"Khiem", 42, 55000};
    return 0;
}

It compiles. So what’s the problem?

  • Everything from UniPerson is copied and pasted.
  • Lecturer has its own next_id, so lecturer and student IDs can clash.
  • Fix a bug in one copy, and you must remember all the others.

2.5 Lecturer inherits from UniPerson

lecturer.h
#ifndef LECTURER_H
#define LECTURER_H

#include "uniperson.h"
#include <string>

class Lecturer : public UniPerson { // a Lecturer IS a UniPerson
  private:
    double salary{}; // only what's new

  public:
    Lecturer(const std::string& name = "", int age = 0, double salary = 42000)
        : UniPerson{name, age}, salary{salary} {}

    double get_salary() const { return salary; }
};

#endif
  • class Lecturer : public UniPerson means “a Lecturer is a UniPerson”. We’ll see what public means here later today.
  • Lecturer only adds what’s new: salary. The member initializer list first passes name and age to UniPerson’s constructor (more on this soon).

2.6 Using Lecturer

main_uniperson_lecturer.cpp
#include "lecturer.h"
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    Lecturer khiem{"Khiem", 42};
    std::cout << khiem.get_name() << ", age " << khiem.get_age() << ", ID "
              << khiem.get_id() << '\n';

    Lecturer albus{"Albus", 115}; // a very experienced lecturer
    std::cout << albus.get_name() << ", age " << albus.get_age() << ", ID "
              << albus.get_id() << '\n';
    return 0;
}
Khiem, age 42, ID 100000
Albus, age 115, ID 100001

We never wrote get_age() or get_id() in Lecturer, yet we can call them: Lecturer inherited them from UniPerson.

2.7 Adding Student is now easy

student.h
#ifndef STUDENT_H
#define STUDENT_H

#include "uniperson.h"
#include <string>

class Student : public UniPerson { // a Student IS a UniPerson
  private:
    double tuition{};

  public:
    Student(const std::string& name = "", int age = 0, double tuition = 9250)
        : UniPerson{name, age}, tuition{tuition} {}

    double get_tuition() const { return tuition; }
};

#endif

2.8 Lecturer and Student together

main_uniperson_lecturer_student.cpp
#include "lecturer.h"
#include "student.h"
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    Lecturer khiem{"Khiem", 42, 55000};
    std::cout << khiem.get_name() << " (ID " << khiem.get_id() << "), salary "
              << khiem.get_salary() << '\n';

    Student peter{"Peter Parker", 18};
    std::cout << peter.get_name() << " (ID " << peter.get_id() << "), tuition "
              << peter.get_tuition() << '\n';
    return 0;
}
Khiem (ID 100000), salary 55000
Peter Parker (ID 100001), tuition 9250

One shared counter: IDs never clash, whether you’re a lecturer or a student.

3 Splitting the program into files

3.1 Why split, and how

A real program has many classes. As in Chapter 02, each class gets:

  • a header file (.h), with the class definition and its member function declarations;
  • an implementation file (.cpp), with the member function definitions.

We’ll build four classes and a main program, in the folder uni-program/:

  • UniPerson;
  • Lecturer and Student, which inherit from UniPerson;
  • UGStudent, which inherits from Student: an inheritance chain.

3.2 UniPerson: the header

uni-program/uniperson.h
#ifndef UNIPERSON_H
#define UNIPERSON_H

#include <string>

class UniPerson {
  private:
    static int next_id; // declared here, defined in uniperson.cpp
    std::string name{};
    int id{};
    int age{};

  public:
    UniPerson(const std::string& name = "", int age = 0);
    const std::string& get_name() const;
    int get_age() const;
    int get_id() const;
};

#endif

Only declarations of the member functions. And the classic way to handle a static member: declare it in the class, and define it once in the .cpp file.

3.3 UniPerson: the implementation

uni-program/uniperson.cpp
#include "uniperson.h"

int UniPerson::next_id{100000}; // the one definition of the counter

UniPerson::UniPerson(const std::string& name, int age)
    : name{name}, id{next_id++}, age{age} {}

const std::string& UniPerson::get_name() const { return name; }
int UniPerson::get_age() const { return age; }
int UniPerson::get_id() const { return id; }
  • Outside the class, every member’s name gets the prefix UniPerson::.
  • int UniPerson::next_id{100000}; is the one definition of the static member. If it were in the header, every .cpp file including the header would define it again: a link error.

3.4 Lecturer: header and implementation

uni-program/lecturer.h
#ifndef LECTURER_H
#define LECTURER_H

#include "uniperson.h"

class Lecturer : public UniPerson {
  private:
    double salary{};

  public:
    Lecturer(const std::string& name = "", int age = 0, double salary = 42000);
    double get_salary() const;
};

#endif
uni-program/lecturer.cpp
#include "lecturer.h"

Lecturer::Lecturer(const std::string& name, int age, double salary)
    : UniPerson{name, age}, salary{salary} {}

double Lecturer::get_salary() const { return salary; }

3.5 Student: header and implementation

uni-program/student.h
#ifndef STUDENT_H
#define STUDENT_H

#include "uniperson.h"

class Student : public UniPerson {
  private:
    double tuition{};

  public:
    Student(const std::string& name = "", int age = 0, double tuition = 9250);
    double get_tuition() const;
};

#endif
uni-program/student.cpp
#include "student.h"

Student::Student(const std::string& name, int age, double tuition)
    : UniPerson{name, age}, tuition{tuition} {}

double Student::get_tuition() const { return tuition; }

3.6 UGStudent: an inheritance chain

uni-program/ugstudent.h
#ifndef UGSTUDENT_H
#define UGSTUDENT_H

#include "student.h"

class UGStudent : public Student { // a chain: UniPerson <- Student <- UGStudent
  public:
    UGStudent(const std::string& name = "", int age = 0, double tuition = 9250);
    void write_bsc_thesis() const;
};

#endif
uni-program/ugstudent.cpp
#include "ugstudent.h"
#include <iostream>

// Default arguments go in the header only (Chapter 05)
UGStudent::UGStudent(const std::string& name, int age, double tuition)
    : Student{name, age, tuition} {}

void UGStudent::write_bsc_thesis() const {
    std::cout << get_name() << " (ID " << get_id()
              << ") is writing a BSc thesis\n";
}

3.7 The main program, and building it

uni-program/main.cpp
#include "lecturer.h"
#include "ugstudent.h"
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    Lecturer khiem{"Khiem", 42, 55000};
    std::cout << khiem.get_name() << " (ID " << khiem.get_id() << "), salary "
              << khiem.get_salary() << '\n';

    UGStudent natasha{"Natasha", 20};
    std::cout << natasha.get_name() << " (ID " << natasha.get_id()
              << "), tuition " << natasha.get_tuition() << '\n';
    natasha.write_bsc_thesis();
    return 0;
}
$ g++ -std=c++20 -Wall main.cpp uniperson.cpp lecturer.cpp student.cpp ugstudent.cpp -o uni
$ ./uni
Khiem (ID 100000), salary 55000
Natasha (ID 100001), tuition 9250
Natasha (ID 100001) is writing a BSc thesis

4 Order of construction

4.1 A base class and a derived class

base_and_derived.cpp
class Base {
  public:
    int id{};

    Base(int id = 0) : id{id} {}
    int get_id() const { return id; }
};

class Derived : public Base { // Derived inherits id and get_id()
  public:
    double value{};

    Derived(double value = 0.0) : value{value} {}
    double get_value() const { return value; }
};

int main() {
    Base base{42};
    Derived derived{42.24};
    return 0;
}

Derived has its own member value, and inherits id and get_id() from Base.

What exactly happens when we create derived?

4.2 A derived object has two parts

The members of Base are not copied into Derived. Instead, a Derived object is made of two parts: a Base part, and a Derived part on top of it.

4.3 The base part is built first

parent_and_child_with_main.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Base {
  public:
    int id{};
    Base(int id = 0) : id{id} { std::cout << "  Base constructed\n"; }
};

class Derived : public Base {
  public:
    double value{};
    Derived(double value = 0.0) : value{value} {
        std::cout << "  Derived constructed\n";
    }
};

int main() {
    std::cout << "Creating a Base:\n";
    Base base{};
    std::cout << "Creating a Derived:\n";
    Derived derived{};
    return 0;
}
Creating a Base:
  Base constructed
Creating a Derived:
  Base constructed
  Derived constructed

Creating a Derived runs the Base constructor first, then the Derived one. It makes sense: the derived part may rely on the base part being ready.

4.4 Inheritance chains

Question: if I create an object of class D, which constructors run, and in which order?

4.5 Construction order in a chain

inheritance_chain_four_classes.cpp
#include <iostream>

class A {
  public:
    A() { std::cout << "  A constructed\n"; }
};

class B : public A {
  public:
    B() { std::cout << "  B constructed\n"; }
};

class C : public B {
  public:
    C() { std::cout << "  C constructed\n"; }
};

class D : public C {
  public:
    D() { std::cout << "  D constructed\n"; }
};

int main() {
    std::cout << "Creating a D:\n";
    D d{};
    return 0;
}
Creating a D:
  A constructed
  B constructed
  C constructed
  D constructed

From the most basic class to the most derived: the great-grandparent A, then the grandparent B, then the parent C, and finally D itself.

5 Constructing derived classes

5.1 Coming from Python: super()

uniperson_super.py
class UniPerson:
    next_id = 100000  # a class variable, like a static member in C++

    def __init__(self, name="", age=18):
        self.name, self.age = name, age
        self.id = UniPerson.next_id
        UniPerson.next_id += 1


class Lecturer(UniPerson):
    def __init__(self, name="", age=18):
        super().__init__(name, age)  # run the parent's constructor first
        print(f"Lecturer {self.name} is recruited.")


khiem = Lecturer("Khiem", 42)
print(f"ID assigned to {khiem.name}: {khiem.id}")
Lecturer Khiem is recruited.
ID assigned to Khiem: 100000

In Python, super().__init__(...) runs the parent’s constructor. How do we do that in C++?

5.2 The problem

initialization_of_derived_class.cpp
class Base {
  public:
    int id{};
    Base(int id = 0) : id{id} {}
};

class Derived : public Base {
  public:
    double value{};
    Derived(double value = 0.0) : value{value} {} // and id?
};

int main() {
    Base base{42};        // Base(int): sets id
    Derived derived{4.2}; // Derived(double): sets value... but id?
    return 0;
}

Derived(double) sets value. But how can it set the id that every Derived inherits from Base?

5.3 What happens when a Derived is created

When Base base{42}; runs:

  1. memory for a Base is set aside;
  2. the right Base constructor is called: its member initializer list initializes the members, then its body runs.

When Derived derived{4.2}; runs:

  1. memory for a whole Derived (both parts) is set aside;
  2. the right Derived constructor is called, but first, the Base part is constructed with a Base constructor. If we don’t say which one, its default constructor is used;
  3. then Derived’s member initializer list and body run.

5.4 Attempt 1: initialize id in Derived’s list

initialization_of_derived_class_approach_01.cpp
class Base {
  public:
    int id{};
    Base(int id = 0) : id{id} {}
};

class Derived : public Base {
  public:
    double value{};
    Derived(double value = 0.0, int id = 0)
        : value{value}, id{id} // error: id is not Derived's own member
    {}
};

int main() {
    Derived derived{4.2, 42};
    return 0;
}
error: class 'Derived' does not have any field named 'id'

A member can only be initialized in the member initializer list of its own class’s constructor. And by then, the Base part (with id) has already been constructed.

5.5 Attempt 2: assign id in the body

initialization_of_derived_class_approach_02.cpp
class Base {
  public:
    const int id{}; // a const member: try removing const
    Base(int id = 0) : id{id} {}
};

class Derived : public Base {
  public:
    double value{};
    Derived(double value = 0.0, int id = 0) : value{value} {
        this->id = id; // error: assigning to a const member
    }
};

int main() {
    Derived derived{4.2, 42};
    return 0;
}
error: assignment of read-only member 'Base::id'

Remove the const and it compiles. But it doesn’t work for const or reference members, and it’s wasteful: id is initialized once by Base, then assigned again.

5.6 The solution: call the base constructor

initialization_of_derived_class_base_constructor.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Base {
  public:
    const int id{}; // const is fine now
    Base(int id = 0) : id{id} {}
};

class Derived : public Base {
  public:
    double value{};
    Derived(double value = 0.0, int id = 0)
        : Base{id}, value{value} // call the Base constructor first
    {}
};

int main() {
    Derived derived{4.2, 42};
    std::cout << "id: " << derived.id << ", value: " << derived.value << '\n';
    return 0;
}
id: 42, value: 4.2

Call the Base constructor first in the member initializer list. It’s C++’s super().__init__().

5.7 Passing values up a chain

initializing_base_members_inheritance_chain.cpp
#include <iostream>

class A {
  public:
    A(int a) { std::cout << "A: " << a << '\n'; }
};

class B : public A {
  public:
    B(int a, double b) : A{a} { std::cout << "B: " << b << '\n'; }
};

class C : public B {
  public:
    C(int a, double b, char c) : B{a, b} { std::cout << "C: " << c << '\n'; }
};

int main() {
    C c{5, 4.3, 'R'}; // C passes a and b up to B; B passes a up to A
    return 0;
}
A: 5
B: 4.3
C: R

Each class calls only its direct parent’s constructor, passing along what that parent needs.

5.8 Destruction: the reverse order

destructor_inheritance_chain.cpp
#include <iostream>

class A {
  public:
    A() { std::cout << "A constructed\n"; }
    ~A() { std::cout << "A destroyed\n"; }
};

class B : public A {
  public:
    B() { std::cout << "B constructed\n"; }
    ~B() { std::cout << "B destroyed\n"; }
};

class C : public B {
  public:
    C() { std::cout << "C constructed\n"; }
    ~C() { std::cout << "C destroyed\n"; }
};

int main() {
    C c{};
    return 0;
} // c is destroyed here
A constructed
B constructed
C constructed
C destroyed
B destroyed
A destroyed

When a derived object is destroyed, the destructors run in reverse order of construction: the most derived part is taken down first.

6 Inheritance and access specifiers

6.1 The protected access specifier

We’ve used public and private. The third access specifier, protected, only matters with inheritance:

  • a protected member can be used by the class itself, its friends, and its derived classes;
  • like a private member, it can’t be used by the public.

Remember the table from Chapter 11? This is its middle column.

6.2 Access specifiers and derived classes

access_specifiers_in_inheritance.cpp
class Base {
  public:
    int public_member{}; // anyone
  protected:
    int protected_member{}; // Base, its friends, derived classes
  private:
    int private_member{}; // Base and its friends only
};

class Derived : public Base {
  public:
    Derived() {
        public_member = 1;    // fine
        protected_member = 2; // fine: Derived is a derived class
        private_member = 3;   // error: private to Base
    }
};

int main() {
    Base base{};
    base.public_member = 1;    // fine
    base.protected_member = 2; // error: main() is "the public"
    return 0;
}
error: 'int Base::private_member' is private within this context
error: 'int Base::protected_member' is protected within this context

Derived can use protected_member, but not private_member. main() can use neither.

6.3 When should we use protected?

With a protected member, every derived class can use it directly. So if we later change it (its type, its meaning, its name), we may have to change every derived class too.

protected makes sense when:

  • we (or our team) are the ones writing the derived classes;
  • there are only a few of them.

In open-source code, anyone can derive from your class and misuse its protected members.

TipBest practice

Favour private members over protected ones. Use protected only when derived classes are planned, and a private member plus public functions would cost too much.

6.4 Kinds of inheritance (read at home)

There are three ways to inherit: public, protected and private. Only public is common; the others are rare.

class Pub : public Base {};    // what we've used all along
class Pro : protected Base {};
class Pri : private Base {};
class Def : Base {};           // defaults to private for a class!

The type of inheritance can make inherited members less accessible:

Member in Base public inheritance protected inheritance private inheritance
public public protected private
protected protected protected private
private inaccessible inaccessible inaccessible

7 Adding, redefining and extending behaviour

7.1 Adding new functionality

base_derived.h
#ifndef BASE_DERIVED_H
#define BASE_DERIVED_H

#include <iostream>

class Base {
  protected:
    int id{};

  public:
    Base(int id = 0) : id{id} {}
    void identify() const { std::cout << "I am a Base, ID " << id << '\n'; }
};

class Derived : public Base {
  private:
    double value{}; // new in Derived

  public:
    Derived(double value = 0.0, int id = 0) : Base{id}, value{value} {}
    void print() const { // new in Derived
        std::cout << "ID " << id << ", value " << value << '\n';
    }
};

#endif

7.2 Using the new functionality

add_functionality_example.cpp
#include "base_derived.h"

int main() {
    Derived derived{24.0, 42};
    derived.identify(); // inherited from Base
    derived.print();    // added by Derived
    return 0;
}
I am a Base, ID 42
ID 42, value 24

One of the biggest benefits of inheritance: reuse what’s written, and add what’s new. A Derived object can use both what it inherited (identify()) and what it added (print()).

7.3 A vector of derived objects

add_functionality_example_vector.cpp
#include "base_derived.h"
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<Derived> list{Derived{42.0, 24}, Derived{24.0, 42}, Derived{}};

    for (const auto& element : list) { // like "for element in list:"
        element.print();
    }
    return 0;
}
ID 24, value 42
ID 42, value 24
ID 0, value 0

for (const auto& element : list) is a range-based for loop: it visits every element of list, like Python’s for element in list:. The const auto& avoids copying each element (Chapter 07).

7.4 Calling a base class function

call_base_class_function.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Base {
  public:
    void identify() const { std::cout << "Base::identify()\n"; }
};

class Derived : public Base {}; // nothing of its own

int main() {
    Base base{};
    base.identify();
    Derived derived{};
    derived.identify(); // the inherited Base::identify()
    return 0;
}
Base::identify()
Base::identify()

Derived inherits identify() from Base, so derived.identify() calls Base::identify().

7.5 Redefining behaviour

redefine_behaviors.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Base {
  public:
    void identify() const { std::cout << "Base::identify()\n"; }
};

class Derived : public Base {
  public:
    void identify() const { std::cout << "Derived::identify()\n"; }
};

int main() {
    Base base{};
    base.identify();
    Derived derived{};
    derived.identify(); // Derived's own version hides Base's
    return 0;
}
Base::identify()
Derived::identify()

If Derived defines its own identify(), a Derived object uses that one instead: it hides the base version.

7.6 Adding to existing behaviour

add_to_existing_functionality.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Base {
  public:
    void identify() const { std::cout << "Base::identify()\n"; }
};

class Derived : public Base {
  public:
    void identify() const {
        std::cout << "Derived::identify()\n";
        Base::identify(); // ...and then do what Base does
    }
};

int main() {
    Derived derived{};
    derived.identify();
    return 0;
}
Derived::identify()
Base::identify()

To extend the base behaviour rather than replace it, call the base version explicitly: Base::identify().

7.7 Changing access with using (read at home)

change_inherited_member_access_level.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Base {
  private:
    int id{};

  public:
    Base(int id) : id{id} {}

  protected:
    void print_id() const { std::cout << "ID " << id << '\n'; }
};

class Derived : public Base {
  public:
    Derived(int id) : Base{id} {}
    using Base::print_id; // protected in Base, public in Derived
};

int main() {
    Derived d{42};
    d.print_id(); // fine now
    return 0;
}
ID 42

A using declaration in the derived class changes an inherited member’s access level. Under public:, using Base::print_id; makes a protected function public.

Under private:, the same trick hides a public member (hide_functionality.cpp). And = delete forbids calling it at all (delete_functions_in_derived.cpp).

8 Multiple inheritance

8.1 Multiple inheritance

Multiple inheritance lets a class inherit from more than one base class.

A Camera can take_photo(); a Phone can make_call(); a SmartPhone is both, and adds apps on top.

8.2 A smartphone in code

multiple_inheritance_smartphone.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

class Camera {
  public:
    void take_photo() const { std::cout << "Taking a photo!\n"; }
};

class Phone {
  public:
    void make_call() const { std::cout << "Making a phone call!\n"; }
};

class SmartPhone : public Camera, public Phone { // two base classes
  public:
    void use_app(const std::string& app) const {
        std::cout << "Using " << app << "!\n";
    }
};

int main() {
    SmartPhone my_phone{};
    my_phone.take_photo(); // from Camera
    my_phone.make_call();  // from Phone
    my_phone.use_app("Moodle");
    return 0;
}
Taking a photo!
Making a phone call!
Using Moodle!
WarningWatch out

Multiple inheritance gets complicated fast: what if both bases have a member with the same name? Use it only when the alternatives are worse.

9 Wrapping up

9.1 Summary

  • Inheritance models “is a”: class Lecturer : public UniPerson. The derived class reuses the base class’s members and adds its own.
  • A derived object has a base part and a derived part. The base part is constructed first and destroyed last; in a chain, from the most basic class to the most derived.
  • Initialize the base part by calling the base constructor first in the member initializer list: C++’s super().__init__().
  • protected members are visible to derived classes, but not to the public. Prefer private.
  • A derived class can add functions, redefine (hide) inherited ones, or extend them by calling Base::function().
  • A class can inherit from several bases, but use that sparingly.
